title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
description: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport . Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that. But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something. So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia. But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

content: AI Updated Nov 9, 2026, 11:51 PM UTC Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang by Richard Lawler The leather-jacketed CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, spurring an investigation by his company and intense discussions worldwide. Recent reporting noted that since last year, US intelligence reports had identified Alice Huang (no relation) as not only the exec for an AI compute company renting access to Nvidia GPUs, but also a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies, including the “neoclouds” like Coreweave who have been some of its biggest customers. So far, Nvidia and Jensen Huang have said that they have “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that hasn’t settled things as the investigation continues. Nov 9 Hayden Field and Lauren Feiner What could China get from Jensen Huang? Image: The Verge It’s difficult to overstate Nvidia’s power in today’s AI landscape. The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump. This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry. Read Article > Nov 9 Jay Peters Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang President Trump held a White House press briefing earlier today and responded to several questions about his knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang said this weekend that he had been “​​unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang . Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May. Read Article > Nov 9 Elizabeth Lopatto The future of AI hinges on… Jensen Huang’s sex life? Step 1. Cut a hole in the box. Image: The Verge I would prefer that these people’s sex lives were none of my business but I guess we have to talk about Jensen Huang and the National Security Incident. Who could have guessed that the guy who was out here signing titties might not have great judgment about how to behave around women ? Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — is a former TV reporter. That was before she became “an executive” at Megaspeed, which bought $4.8 billion of hard-to-get Nvidia chips, starting around the time she was being photographed with Jensen in a Taipei bar in 2024. “To many in the industry, the well-funded push by Megaspeed into A.I. appeared to come out of nowhere,” The New York Times wrote, tactfully . Our girl Alice is also an alleged honeypot who was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security. ( China is denying all this, btw.) Read Article > Nov 8 Terrence O'Brien Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, at media briefing in July 2026. Photo: Bloomberg via Getty Images On Sunday, Nvidia announced it was launching an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an AI executive and agent of the Chinese government. In addition to the Board of Directors announcing the investigation, Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees acknowledging the affair. You can read the full text below. content: Policy AI Report Jonathan Kanter is using AI to take on Big Tech The former DOJ watchdog wants to fuel antitrust cases against all kinds of monopolists. The former DOJ watchdog wants to fuel antitrust cases against all kinds of monopolists. by Lauren Feiner Nov 9, 2026, 2:30 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Lauren Feiner is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform. When Jonathan Kanter stepped down as head of the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division in 2024, he set out to keep fighting to dismantle illegal monopolies. But this time, he’s continuing the fight in the private sector, and with a perhaps unexpected tool: AI. Alongside former acting Antitrust Division chief Doha Mekki, Kanter recently launched a new tech startup, FluxCap . The team is stacked with former DOJ staffers and former Palantir engineers, and it’s selling an AI-based legal research and analysis tool that helps plaintiffs build and strengthen cases against the kinds of well-heeled companies Kanter and Mekki took on at the Antitrust Division. FluxCap is launching with a focus on antitrust cases, but it plans to expand into other practice areas as well. Kanter imagines FluxCap as a “force multiplier” for antitrust watchdogs taking on powerful opponents in Big Tech and elsewhere. “This, to me, it’s existential” “This, to me, it’s existential,” he tells The Verge in an interview. “Because it’s the only way that enforcement is going to work in the long term, is if technology and other tools are able to help scarce resources go significantly further than they can today.” FluxCap’s platform, built off proprietary technology and existing large language models, is primarily intended for research and analysis. It’s trained to pick up the facts and legal framework that will determine whether a case succeeds, then find potential holes in attorneys’ logic. To help attorneys prepare for trial, FluxCap can also help sift through vast piles of discovery materials, searching for signals that a company acted in anticompetitive ways. It’s part of a wave of legal tech tools that are using AI to try to help lawyers do more with less and make the legal process more efficient. Getting the tool to find relevant evidence was one of the hardest parts, Kanter says. Executives are unlikely to come out and say they’re monopolists, but surrounding context can give a very specific meaning to certain messages. In the antitrust trial against Live Nation-Ticketmaster, for example, the government played a recorded phone call between the Live Nation CEO and a customer who decided to switch to a different ticketing platform. In response, the CEO reminded the customer that a new arena in town could make it harder to deliver as many concerts to his venue. The customer testified he took it as a “not-so-veiled” threat that Live Nation could cut off events programming if he didn’t also accept its ticketing service. FluxCap’s team of former government lawyers spent months testing the system with existing and hypothetical test cases to see if it could really help build a solid argument. Getting “basic legal tools” (which Kanter calls “BLTs”) to understand that kind of nuance is difficult because “lawyering isn’t about right or wrong answers,” he says. “Both sides can be right and both sides can be wrong. And what you’re essentially trying to do is you’re trying to persuade a court, a jury, a regulator to reach a certain outcome.” The team counts antitrust boutique firm Kressin Powers as one of its first customers , and Kanter says it’s in talks with both public and private enforcers. “It gives them that virtual capacity so that a small team can take on a large team,” Kanter says, adding that it provides the manpower of roughly “20-plus people working around the clock.” The seeds of FluxCap began inside the Antitrust Division, where Kanter and his team were already trying to stretch their limited resources with technology. During the Biden administration, the DOJ went to trial against Google twice and brought monopolization suits against Apple and Live Nation, among other actions. But the Division’s resources and staff pale in comparison to companies with multibillion- to trillion-dollar market caps and large legal teams to review documents and mount defenses. The entire Antitrust Division was appropriated $245 million by Congress for fiscal year 2026, with more than 400 attorneys on staff across several issue areas. “It’s just not realistic to have the resources necessary to take on these big companies” The imbalance is even greater for state attorneys general, who have pushed forward with antitrust action as the Trump administration has hung back. Earlier this year, state AGs won a case against Live Nation that the DOJ under the Trump administration settled, and states also sued to block the Paramount-Warner Media merger before ultimately settling, when the DOJ declined. “A large state AG might have 10 people working on a case,” Kanter says. “It’s just not realistic to have the resources necessary to take on these big companies.” During Kanter’s time as antitrust head, he and others tried AI-based BLTs but found them lacking for complex legal research. “Every antitrust lawyer has tried asking questions to ChatGPT or [AI legal research software] Harvey or one of those tools, and they do okay,” Kanter says. “But they miss the nuance.” While Kanter was at the DOJ, the Antitrust Division secured a $45.5 million grant from the government’s Tech Modernization Fund to implement better tools for managing cases and reviewing evidence. Kanter says his team “never had the opportunity to put that to work” before leaving office, but what they’re building now is “even more ambitious and better than I could have imagined when I was at DOJ.” Tech alone can’t fully even the playing field, Kanter says. “Government is always going to be outmatched, and they desperately need more funding, and desperately need more budget, and more headcount.” Even if that happens, however, private defendants are likely to “far outweigh anything that the government could ever produce, whether it’s federal government or states or private plaintiffs,” he says. “We believe this will be the great equalizer that will allow those teams to go toe to toe with anyone regardless of their size and regardless how deep their pockets are.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. content: Exploring the world's languages with Language Explorer November 9, 2026 Daan van Esch, Senior Technical Program Manager, Google DeepMind and Uche Okonkwo, Senior Program Manager, Google Research Language Explorer, featured in an exhibition at the Museum of Communication in Berlin, Germany, lets you explore the world's linguistic diversity online through visualizations and data. Quick links Language Explorer site Exhibition online companion Share Our world has a fascinating wealth of languages, and for over two decades, Google has been building language technologies that cover as many languages as possible. In 2006, we started a small experiment with Google Translate, supporting just two languages (English and Arabic) at the time. Fast forward to today: nearly 250 languages are supported, with around a trillion words translated every month . Our commitment to linguistic diversity runs across products, all in service of our mission to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful. Building products that reflect the world's linguistic diversity takes far more than software engineering; it requires close collaboration with the communities we aim to serve, building in a way that's deeply aligned and respectful of local communities, heritage, history, values and context. This is why we've been working on grassroots initiatives like Project Vaani in India and Project Waxal in Africa, partnering with local organizations to collect thousands of hours of open speech data across underserved languages. But gathering this data is only one part of the journey. Preserving language vitality requires working closely with native speakers, academic institutions, and cultural organizations. Partnerships, such as our coalition with the Gates Foundation , ensure that modern digital tools reflect the nuances and authentic voices of their communities. Expanding language coverage responsibly also requires deeply understanding linguistic diversity on a global scale. This approach enables products like Gboard , our Android keyboard, to support 900+ language varieties. To better appreciate the breadth and complexity of this speech diversity, we've been working on a tool to help visualize the world's linguistic diversity, inspired by earlier visualization initiatives like Google Earth . The Language Explorer is an interactive web platform designed to let researchers, educators, and language enthusiasts discover and visualize linguistic diversity around the world. Developed as part of our 1,000 Languages Initiative , the Language Explorer brings together data across thousands of languages, building on our open-source LinguaMeta dataset . play looping video pause looping video unmute video mute video This week marks the opening of a new major exhibition at the Museum of Communication Berlin, Real Talk! Language. Power. World. ( Real Talk! Sprache. Macht. Welt. ) featuring the Language Explorer as an interactive installation. The exhibition explores how language shapes identity, society, and technology across a multi-year run in Berlin (through February 2028) and at the Museum of Communication Frankfurt (through September 2029). The Language Explorer installation reflects our broader work to build AI and language technologies that serve everyone, regardless of what language they speak, read, or sign . If you can't make it to the exhibition in person, you can explore the museum's themes via an online companion starting November 6th, or dive directly into the world's rich linguistic diversity online with the Language Explorer . title: Anthropic joins AI’s natural gas frenzy, buys $3.4B worth of turbines
description: Anthropic bought billions of dollars' worth of natural gas turbines in a deal that could give it buyer's remorse.
content: AI’s power crunch has become so acute that Anthropic, a company that has generally avoided buying physical infrastructure, is spending $3.4 billion on natural gas turbines. The AI company, which is planning to go public this year, is buying Caterpillar generators that equipment supplier OnePWR had originally ordered, according to a Financial Times report . The generators are capable of producing up to 1.7 gigawatts of electricity. Historically, Anthropic has preferred to rent rather than buy. The company disclosed in its S-1 filing in May that it is paying SpaceX subsidiary xAI $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 to use xAI’s computing power. “We expect to enter into additional similar services contracts,” Anthropic stated in the filing, meaning more deals to rent computing power. But as demand for compute ramps up, the market for power has also grown increasingly uncertain, which may have forced its hand. The backlog for natural gas turbines stretches into the early 2030s, and queues to connect to the electrical grid can be just as long. Anthropic’s purchase looks like a last resort. According to the report, OnePWR ordered the turbines a couple years ago but couldn’t find financing to complete the purchase. Anthropic had planned to buy them from OnePWR but instead went directly to Caterpillar, the manufacturer. It’s not clear why OnePWR was unable to secure financing despite Anthropic’s apparent interest as a customer. Whatever the case, Anthropic likely wanted to keep the generating capacity to itself rather than give a competitor an opportunity to snap it up. AI companies have been ramping up their purchases of natural gas equipment and supplies in recent years. Google , Amazon , Microsoft , and Meta have all announced plans to build massive natural gas power plants to power their data centers on-site, rather than drawing from the public grid. The binge has given a second wind to fracking , the drilling method used to extract natural gas from underground rock. And if the buildout proceeds as planned, U.S. data centers alone could consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined by 2035. The reliance on natural gas also exposes hyperscalers to price fluctuations. One analyst expects that prices could more than triple by the end of the decade in some markets. If that happens, Anthropic might have a serious case of buyer’s remorse. content: Tech AI News Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang In a White House press conference, President Trump was vague about when learned of Jensen Huang’s affair. In a White House press conference, President Trump was vague about when learned of Jensen Huang’s affair. by Jay Peters Nov 9, 2026, 11:47 PM UTC Part Of Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang see all updates Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme. President Trump held a White House press briefing earlier today and responded to several questions about his knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang said this weekend that he had been “​​unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang . Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May. In the press conference, Trump wasn’t specific about when he learned of the affair. But Trump said Huang told him today that he had “no idea” the person was a spy. Here are Trump’s responses to questions about Jensen Huang from his press briefing today. You can watch a replay of the press conference on MS Now’s YouTube channel . When were you first informed that there was an issue with Jensen Huang and the affair? What was presented to you at the time? I would say that when I heard about it, first of all, I was amazed because I view him as a very high-quality person. I’ve known him a long time. It’s the largest, by value, the largest or one of the largest companies in the world. He did that with a chip. When you think about it, you’ve got a chip that’s 10 years advanced, can’t be… the Blackwell can’t even be copied. He’s an amazing guy. I just hope there’s no problem. If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it. But I hope there’s no problem. I believe he’s suffering greatly. I read his statement. And I believe he’s suffering greatly. Moreso because of his family. His wife who he loves and his family. But he is definitely suffering. Just to follow up on the, “When were you first told of these potential issues with Mr. Huang?” You didn’t answer that question. Well I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago. When is that? We’ll look into it. I know the FBI’s looking into it in terms of something else. I think that he’ll be in good shape. … Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him next week? No, I don’t think so. Maybe, I’m sure, President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man. He built a great company. American company. I think he’s a very honorable guy. I feel very confident that he’ll be in good shape. Sticking with Jensen Huang, when you went to China earlier this year in May, did you know about these alleged ties to the spy then? No, I didn’t hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it. And Jensen totally denies that. I asked him today, because I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling alright, how are you doing… and I asked him about that. He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy. I asked him that question, did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said, I had no idea that she was a spy. And I really believe him. … I want to put a finer point on when exactly you were made aware of the intelligence around Jensen Huang. Oh, I’d have to check. But this has been going on… But there are reports that Secretary Rubio put an intelligence memo out last year. Did you read that memo? I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me. Logic Pro is Apple’s first app to charge for extended usage of Apple Intelligence. by Andrew Liszewski Nov 9, 2026, 7:09 PM UTC Image: Apple Andrew Liszewski is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid. After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac . It has a built-in AI assistant to do things like “start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.” These Intelligence Usage Packs, as Apple calls them, will allow users to continue accessing certain Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits because they rely on cloud-based AI models from OpenAI or Google Gemini. The Usage Packs can only be used by the Apple Account that purchased them (Family Sharing isn’t supported) and, as Apple explains on its website , any unused additional usage will roll over from month to month, but will expire 12 months after it was purchased. For Logic Pro, Apple says the usage limit is “impacted by the complexity of conversations you have with the assistant.” Users finding themselves running out of access can find the option to buy an Intelligence Usage Pack in the Intelligence Features > Show Usage section of the app’s main menu. Currently, only Logic Pro has the option to buy more usage, but it’s expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers that are getting access to Apple’s AI chatbot . title: A short seller flagged Nvidia CEO’s ties to a suspected Chinese spy six months before the scandal
description: Six months before Nvidia's spy scandal erupted, Culper Research was already questioning Jensen Huang's unusually close relationship with a Chinese executive.
content: Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged , the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. She is now suspected to be a Chinese spy. The Nvidia CEO admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and the company has now opened a formal investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang (who shares his last name but is not related). U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips. Culper’s May 13 report is resurfacing because it picked up on the connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang while investigating Megaspeed’s ties to Nvidia. NEW: We are short Nvidia $NVDA . We believe Nvidia has a significant China problem. Please see our full report and disclosures now available on our website, link in bio. pic.twitter.com/oTaJyL7S2R — Culper (@CulperResearch) May 13, 2026 In particular, the report called the relationship between the two executives “uncomfortably close,” noting that the Nvidia CEO was spotted partying and socializing with Alice Huang on multiple occasions. The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.” Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies. It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source. Financial Times reported Monday that documents show Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries. Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. title: The race is on to sue Nvidia
description: Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% after its board opened an investigation into Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, and one securities law expert says the company’s earlier insistence that it was all “normal” could turn into a very expensive problem.
content: Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% on Monday, the first trading day after its board said it would investigate CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive U.S. intelligence believes was spying for China. Securities lawyers were already moving. At least four firms, including Schall, Brown & Schwartz and Levi & Korsinsky, announced investigations Monday into whether Nvidia misled investors. Robert Bartlett, a Stanford Law professor and securities law expert, expects them to have plenty of company. “I would definitely wager that there’ll be a filing,” Bartlett said in an interview Monday morning, adding that he wouldn’t be surprised if a case had been filed by the end of the day. Plaintiffs’ lawyers have good reasons to be first in line; under federal securities law, the first complaint triggers a public notice, and investors then have 60 days to ask the court to be named lead plaintiff. A firm that files early gets a head start on signing up investors with large losses, as well as on shaping the story of the case. Bartlett was right, in fact. A case surfaced Monday afternoon in the Northern District of California, where Nvidia is headquartered. Rosen Law Firm, a New York-based plaintiffs’ firm that specializes in securities class actions, filed it on behalf of Mark Kistenmacher, a retail investor who made seven purchases totaling roughly $20,500 this year, according to a schedule attached to the complaint. (Rosen was lead counsel in a $250 million settlement with Alibaba and ranks among the most active filers of such cases.) The proposed class covers anyone who bought Nvidia securities between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026, and the suit names both Nvidia and Huang. The complaint accuses them of misleading investors about Huang’s ties to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center outfit where Alice Huang was considered a top exec, and it points to three statements as proof: Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo’s late-October claim that Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected,” the company’s even earlier claim that it found “ no evidence of diversion ” of its chips, and Jensen Huang’s Oct. 30 comment to Bloomberg that Nvidia’s dealings with Megaspeed were “ normal and not unusual .” All three were false or misleading, the suit says, because Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang. Kistenmacher is asking for unspecified damages, interest and attorneys’ fees, and he wants a jury trial. While much remains unknown, the legal theory here doesn’t depend on anything the board’s investigation may turn up about Huang’s private life. When The New York Times first reported on Huang’s ties to Alice Huang last month, Rizzo really did tell the Times that the relationship was “ not unusual or unexpected .” Rizzo separately told another outlet , The Hill, that “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” Of course, the world now knows that was not true. Worse, the Times reports that U.S. intelligence had been monitoring Alice Huang for more than a year. From a securities perspective, Bartlett said, the company’s earlier statement was “clearly a misleading statement.” And because Huang is CEO, Bartlett said, “his knowledge gets imputed to the company.” In other words, Nvidia is treated as having known what its chief executive knew. The Kistenmacher complaint makes the same argument. Bartlett predicted a “classic fraud on the market” claim, in which investors argue they paid prices that reflected false or incomplete public information, and lost money when the truth emerged. This early lawsuit relies on that theory, and Monday’s drop of $7.97 per share, or 4.27%, gives the attorneys involved a lot to work with. Damages in such cases are tied to the stock’s decline, and Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world, so you can imagine a settlement could prove exceedingly expensive. That means a large payment from the company and its directors-and-officers insurers, but typically no personal consequences for the CEO or the board. It is also a civil matter, so Huang isn’t facing prison over it. The irony, as Bartlett noted, is that the suit is brought in the name of Nvidia’s shareholders, and shareholders ultimately pay for the settlement, directly or through insurance premiums. Bartlett sorted Nvidia’s wider exposure into buckets. The first is the securities fraud claim, which is the clearest immediate problem for the company and potentially for Huang. The second is governance: what the board knew and when. It’s possible directors were kept in the dark, but the board also has oversight duties, and once the Times began reporting on the Megaspeed connection, the company should have had reporting lines to bring a critical risk like this to directors. If it didn’t, or if directors didn’t act, board-level liability is possible. A third category, one that would change everything, would arise only if the board’s investigation finds Huang knew about the intelligence connection. That would be “a whole other ball game,” as Bartlett said. (The board said in a statement to the public Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.) There’s also the question of government action. The SEC can seek an officer-and-director bar for intentional securities-fraud violations, which Bartlett said is technically on the table. But he doubts the current SEC under Chairman Paul Atkins would have the appetite, given President Trump’s support for Huang. A roughly two-year clock after discovery of the facts would leave room for a future administration to act, but the window would be tight, and Bartlett posited that’s pretty unlikely when asked about it. It’s worth underscoring that neither law firm announcements nor this newly filed complaint is a sign of a strong case. Plaintiffs’ firms are quick to publish these notices when they see an opportunity. Which firm winds up leading the case is decided later by the court, and that decision usually depends on which investor has suffered the biggest loss. Kistenmacher said in his filing that he’s willing to serve as lead plaintiff, but the court will ultimately choose among the competing investors. No doubt they’ll materialize soon. content: November 10, 2026 Models Gemini Robotics 2.5 accelerates real-world general dexterity Carolina Parada Your browser does not support the video tag. We’re enabling robots to learn faster for the real world - from everyday skills to the factory floor Today, we are introducing Gemini Robotics 2.5, our most capable vision-language-action (VLA) model to date. Gemini Robotics 2.5 increases both the breadth of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it can acquire them. This enhances dexterity, reliability, and safety to help robots step out of the lab and into more unstructured, real-world environments, where they can assist people with a greater range of tasks. Earlier this year, we brought whole-body intelligence to robots of many types, including humanoids. Now, in large part thanks to Gemini 4 Argon's ability to accelerate robotics research, we have further pushed the frontier of physical intelligence. We tested Gemini Robotics 2.5’s capabilities in task breadth, performance, and complexity across over 200 distinct tasks, though this approach could scale to many more. Gemini Robotics 2.5 marks a leap forward in three key areas: Dexterity: Our robots can perform significantly more tasks with greater performance and dexterity — from using everyday tools to handling delicate, flexible objects. Reliability: During a real-world proof-of-concept on Mercedes-Benz production lines, our models helped Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid pick and pack automotive parts with a 96% success rate. This could enable robots to take on monotonous work, to enable technicians to focus on complex build tasks. Safety: As robots move into everyday environments, we have improved physical safety steerability and introduced a new benchmark to test against adversarial jailbreaks specific to robotics. Gemini Robotics 2.5 is rolling out to our robotics partners . Your browser does not support the video tag. Your browser does not support the video tag. Expanding task breadth, reliability, and dexterity Because real-world environments are unstructured and unpredictable, robots must be able to handle everyday objects with both fine precision and high reliability. With Gemini Robotics 2.5, we expanded the model capabilities in task breadth, performance, and complexity. We evaluated the model across 200 distinct tasks — such as serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box, and pipetting a liquid. These tasks represent a step toward human-level dexterity by combining a number of skills, including advanced tool use, complex manipulation of deformables, and handling delicate objects with finesse. Our evaluations show significant increases in task precision, robustness, and speed. Compared to previous baselines, Gemini Robotics 2.5 achieves a 30% to 100% higher success rate depending on the type of task, while completing tasks 20% to 30% faster. Like our previous Gemini Robotics models, it natively works with many different robot types, including Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot (featuring the five-finger, 22 degree-of-freedom SharpaWave hand) and the Franka Duo platform with two-fingered parallel grippers. Slide 1 of 4 Testing real-world reliability with Apptronik’s Apollo and Mercedes-Benz The ultimate measure of a robotics model is whether it can perform dependably in an active workplace. To put Gemini Robotics 2.5 to the test, we partnered with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz to use Apollo 2 humanoid robots on active automotive production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. Robots struggle to adapt to new unpredictable environments, our Gemini Robotics models give Apollo the ability to think, reason over multiple steps, and take action adapting to changes. In this proof-of-concept, Apollo 2 autonomously performs automotive kitting: the repetitive, physically taxing task of sorting individual parts from bulk bins into organized trays in the exact order needed for each vehicle on the line. Offloading this monotonous prep work helps keep the assembly line moving, while freeing up technicians to focus on complex build tasks. Using our embodied reasoning model ( Gemini Robotics ER ) to keep track of the workflow, and the Gemini Robotics 2.5 actions model to control its hands and arms, the robot reaches into supply bins, picks up metal automotive brackets, and places them into sequencing containers, all while correcting for any gaps. Achieving a 96% success rate, this pilot shows promising progress toward widespread real-world industrial applications. This is what we built Apollo for: useful work alongside people in real industrial settings. Pairing Apollo 2 with Gemini Robotics, we saw the models improve dramatically in just a few weeks of post-training and carry over to Mercedes-Benz production with very little drop-off. This is the foundation for bringing humanoid robots to industrial and commercial environments at scale. Jeff Cardenas Co-founder and CEO, Apptronik Your browser does not support the video tag. Apollo 2 using Gemini Robotics 2.5 to autonomously perform automotive kitting at a Mercedes-Benz factory. Advancing steerability and agentic safety for robots As robots operate in messy, everyday spaces, physical safety is paramount. To help ensure this, we have significantly advanced Gemini Robotics 2.5’s safety features. Gemini Robotics 2.5 uses inference-time reasoning guidance to steer around physical hazards in real-time. Much like safety classifiers add a protective layer around Gemini’s responses, this guidance allows the robot to navigate complex environments securely. In our evaluations, this capability boosted safe task completion around obstacles by 33% and around nearby people by 43%. We are also advancing safety for long-horizon, agentic tasks. Gemini 4 Argon currently leads our agentic robotics evaluations across unsafe task refusal, resolving uncertainty, and working in proximity to humans. To test jailbreak robustness, we are releasing ASIMOV-Jailbreak , a new open-source benchmark containing hundreds of prompts that disguise unsafe requests across dozens of scenes. Argon achieves a 99.5% jailbreak resistance — a significant improvement over the 82% rate of our previous baseline, Gemini Robotics ER 2. Your browser does not support the video tag. Safe human-aware robot actions enabled by GR-2.5 steerability Accelerating robotics with Gemini 4 Argon To teach robots new skills, researchers need massive amounts of physical data and highly efficient modeling algorithms. Gemini 4 Argon’s robotics research capabilities helped solve these bottlenecks by acting as a simulation engine, which greatly accelerated our development of Gemini Robotics 2.5. Examples of Gemini 4 Argon’s robotics research capabilities accelerating Gemini Robotics 2.5 Argon can generate thousands of varied, simulated practice runs from a real-world camera scene and build a realistic digital twin. Combined with real training demonstrations, this enables the robot to more quickly generalize to new scenes and objects. Argon can also help researchers hypothesize why task failures happen from video footage and test the best improvements both in simulation and directly on real robots. Accelerated by frontier intelligence models like Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini Robotics 2.5 marks an important milestone on the path toward solving physical AGI. title: Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution
description: At 10 cents per million input tokens, Ember is significantly cheaper than frontier competitors like Haiku and Luna.
content: Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet. In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.” Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna. Image Credits: Meta Superintelligence Labs At 10 cents per million input tokens, Ember is significantly cheaper than frontier competitors like Haiku and Luna. Not only that, it’s cost-competitive with open source competitors like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash. Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness. In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.” With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio. The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video without a separate model.” Ember is the fourth model released under Meta’s Muse brand, following the mid-weight Spark ( released in April ), Spark’s open source twin Glimmer ( released in August ), and the Wonder frontier model ( released in October ). content: Anthropic released new versions of its most advanced models on Monday, with the launch of Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2. The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users. Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens. As a result, Fable 5.2 is now cheaper than its primary competitor GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels. Faster inference serving is available for double the price. Fable 5.2 is also compatible with zero data retention (ZDR) policies through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system , long a sticking point for many enterprise clients. It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR , which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found internal models were speeding up Anthropic’s AI progress by roughly 2x, although many uncertainties remain. Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.” Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a verdict that’s detailed further in Mythos 5.2’s system card . “Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor,” the system card reads. “That said, we believe that low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations.” Fable 5.2 has been available to select parties in pre-release for some time, and Anthropic says the model has already “solved two open problems in theoretical physics, formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem, and supported numerous other research projects.” Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing. Notably, the lab said the result was achieved by running “a non-public Anthropic model” within PSI’s own system. Anthropic did not confirm or deny whether Fable 5.2 was the model in question. title: Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s ‘about a 50-50’
description: Nvidia’s board is investigating Jensen Huang over his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, and Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld thinks it’s roughly a coin flip whether Huang stays on as CEO.
content: Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. But this isn’t a case of just another CEO having an extramarital affair. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry ,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down. A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “ groundless smears and slanders ,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and it isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised. The question is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought. First, the damage. Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted. But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.” Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits , if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that people earn latitude in a group by showing competence and following its rules. Huang has been earning latitude since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. But all that goodwill can run out when a screw-up looks self-serving or touches the group’s core norms. Here that group includes Nvidia’s board, its roughly 42,000 employees who are bound by security rules, and, in a looser sense, the U.S. government, given it restricts its exports. We also talked about precedents, except, as it turns out, there really are none for what’s unfolding right now. Executives who survive personal scandals sometimes pick up where they left off at another company, Sonnenfeld observed. Former HP CEO Mark Hurd is one example. Between 2005 and 2010, he drove HP to the top of the tech industry by revenue, then was pressured to resign after he filed inaccurate expense reports that hid a personal relationship with a contractor. Oracle hired him about a month later. Huang has no equivalent because Nvidia is his company As for the bench at Nvidia, that doesn’t really exist either. While there is typically a hierarchy inside companies of Nvidia’s scale and importance, Huang has kept things as flat as possible, with about 60 direct reports by his own account. That structure makes it hard to figure out who would succeed him (though his children, both of whom work at Nvidia, are sometimes the subject of succession speculation ). That won’t stop the worldwide guessing game that’s sure to follow. And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea. Nvidia’s role at the center of a massive and complex circular financing web is what makes this particular predicament so tricky and, undoubtedly, terrifying for a wide number of constituents. Nvidia isn’t just the biggest provider of chips driving the AI boom but also largely the bank behind the buildout. In addition to stakes in hundreds of smaller startups, Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave, and Nebius. In August, it also signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion over time, and Huang has said Nvidia could backstop up to a quarter of it. The move was widely interpreted as a way to spread risk. Now, a leadership crisis at the center is how a stumble becomes a collapse. So what’s Nvidia’s board likely doing at this moment? Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s constant, public advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, whose company Nvidia has backed, had a lot to say about selling chips to China at Davos back in January, likening it to “ selling nuclear weapons to North Korea .” Now the board’s independent members — meaning everyone but Huang — will have to establish what technology reached China if any, and by what routes, including by better understanding Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed. The Singapore cloud company, which grew out of a Chinese gaming business and became Nvidia’s largest buyer in Southeast Asia, bought roughly $2 billion of its chips , The New York Times reported in October 2025, raising broader questions about whether it was helping China circumvent U.S. export restrictions by re-exporting the chips to China or renting them to Chinese customers remotely. (An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill after the Times report that the allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year .”) In the meantime, Huang will keep running the company, Nvidia said Sunday. That’ll be a tall order, even for a CEO who already spends much of his time traveling the world to promote Nvidia. For starters, three House chairmen want a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18. Nvidia is also reporting its newest earnings on November 17. Sonnenfeld expects that even if Huang keeps the title, he’ll have to hand off some of the day-to-day decision-making. Only one thing is certain right now. Huang doesn’t own the kind of super-voting stock that would cement his power at Nvidia. Sonnenfeld often argues for dual-class structures that empower founders, and he says Huang’s success without one has been the best counterargument to that case. But if Huang had one, Sonnenfeld continued, removing him would be harder. This episode may be remembered as a pivotal moment for how the tech industry guards its secrets. Sonnenfeld argues tech has been “way too lax” compared with defense contractors that face clearance regimes. The arrest last month of an OpenAI engineer points to the same problem. He was accused of hiding a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room, and while OpenAI has said it has no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were accessed, the case highlights how exposed tech companies are to people who get close. Huang may well survive the investigation (Sonnenfeld hopes the board clears him of knowingly aiding anyone). The bigger test comes when Nvidia’s employees, customers, and partners, and, indirectly, the millions of Americans with Nvidia in their 401(k) plans, have to decide whether an AI economy built largely on the judgment of Huang still makes sense. title: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny
description: Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy threatens to complicate Nvidia’s lobbying efforts to loosen U.S. chip export restrictions and maintain access to China’s lucrative AI market.
content: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology. The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument. The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday. U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions. Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers . The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia. Historically, China has been a big market for the company. It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives. In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue. Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to expand access to China , and some of his persuasion tactics have been successful. Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors. On numerous occasions, Huang has publicly lamented export controls, calling them a “ failure ” at a conference last year and saying in May that it was “ not wise ” for the U.S. and China to create two distinct AI ecosystems. He has also warned that shutting Nvidia out of China’s compute market would enable the country to develop its own AI chips to challenge Nvidia internationally. China is already moving in that direction. Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China. Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead. The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024. At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets. Still, the allegations involving Alice Huang open new scrutiny of the company’s business relationships and could taint any assurances Nvidia offers that it can prevent sensitive technology from reaching unauthorized customers. Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly warned officials close to Trump earlier this year about Huang’s relationship with an alleged spy. Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China. title: Automattic debuts a platform to deploy vibe-coding apps amid a changing internet
description: Automattic aims to compete with the likes of Lovable with Spacefast.
content: WordPress has been a crucial technology and content management system for websites like TechCrunch. Now, WordPress.com owner Automattic is responding to the changing state of the web by debuting a new service called Spacefast , which will allow users to deploy vibe-coded websites and apps. Spacefast is designed to provide infrastructure for the vibe-coded apps, including databases, authentication, file uploads, emails, and analytics, to make them functional websites, apps, or services. The product competes with the likes of Lovable and Emergent, which offer both interface and rails for vibe-coded apps, but in a more open way. Users can connect Spacefast with other agents and chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, Hermes, OpenClaw, Grok Bot, Muse, Pi, Cursor, OpenCode, and Amp. Alternatively, they can connect a Git repository to Spacefast to get started. The product is headed by Batuhan İçöz, who worked on it during one of the company’s hackathon sprints earlier in the year. At that time, he worked on the company’s cross-platform messaging app Beeper and said that he often got Vercel links from his non-technical friends while exploring vibe coding. “I thought there had to be a better way for everyone to set up and deploy their projects. Automattic already has good infrastructure, but we have been traditionally associated with just WordPress. I thought, why do I have to use Cloudflare when we have a CDN (content delivery network) just as good? So I started working on what was called Stattic and now Spacefast,” he told TechCrunch over a call. An Office-themed game on Spacefast Image Credits: Spacefast İçöz eventually disseminated the solution to his friends and added more features to make the product more dynamic. Automattic soft-launched the product in September to get feedback before today’s launch. The company has seen varied use cases of their product, with people and organizations using it for internal mockups, slideshows, and offer-related websites. However, that’s not the only competition Spacefast has. Productivity and design software like Figma, Canva, and Notion have launched products that sit at the intersection of vibe coding, mockups, and presentations. İçöz thinks that, compared to something like Lovable, Spacefast has the advantage of giving users a choice of their agent and using the solution their way. The counter-argument might be that a certain kind of user wouldn’t want to choose and just have everything figured out for them. Spacefast said that it also has the advantage of being within Automattic to launch solutions like web analytics, WordPress integration, and e-commerce features (through WooCommerce) easily to compete better with the whole lot. “For enterprises, the problem right now is IT sprawl, as their marketing teams are churning out landing pages on services like Lovable, and they want to consolidate and work with a company that understands the enterprise needs. With our existing products, we have experience serving enterprise customers,” İçöz noted. A Saturday morning TV-styled YouTube experince on Spacefast Image Credits: Spacefast A challenge for newly minted products in the AI world is to retain people post-launch. Users might get excited to try out a new product, and then move on to the new shiny thing within days or weeks. İçöz is cognizant of the fact and said that he expects people to churn, as they might not be interested in making apps at all. “I think what we need to do as a product is make sure that when you build something with SpaceFast, it is so easy, and the results are so much better than without Spacefast,” İçöz emphasized. Many websites and publishers are struggling with dwindling traffic due to AI chatbots and summaries, right now, to the point that Google itself saw its ad revenue growth drop . İçöz acknowledged that people are making websites with ChatGPT or Claude now as compared to deploying something on WordPress, and he said some sites won’t need a content management system at all as the web expands. Spacefast comes amid turbulent months at Automattic. In an OpenAI/Sam Altman-style saga, the company’s board forced CEO Matt Mullenweg out , but he was back in control within days . The rebel board was eventually replaced , and the interim CFO left within weeks of appointment. In October, TechCrunch reported that the company had begun layoffs across several properties and more cuts were expected. content: AI Gadgets Policy What could China get from Jensen Huang? The Nvidia CEO has been in a unique position to to influence AI export controls. by Hayden Field and Lauren Feiner Nov 9, 2026, 11:51 PM UTC Image: The Verge AI Gadgets Policy What could China get from Jensen Huang? The Nvidia CEO has been in a unique position to to influence AI export controls. by Hayden Field and Lauren Feiner Nov 9, 2026, 11:51 PM UTC Part Of Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang see all updates It’s difficult to overstate Nvidia’s power in today’s AI landscape. The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump. This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry. Huang is in hot water after news broke of his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider and a top Nvidia customer. Questions are swirling around how the affair may have influenced Huang’s reported push to sell advanced chips to China — and potentially even influenced President Trump’s own decisions surrounding AI export controls. Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry US officials believe the Megaspeed executive is a foreign intelligence asset that has funneled information straight to the Chinese government, per The New York Times — in particular, officials reportedly believe that Megaspeed is related to a convoluted web of Chinese companies working together to access chips in bulk and perhaps even illegally get some of those chips into China. Alibaba is reportedly one of Megaspeed’s top customers. “It’s not entirely surprising that the CEO of arguably one of the most important, if not the most important, AI chip companies is the target of some sort of intelligence-gathering from countries like China,” Hanna Dohmen, a senior research analyst at CSET, said in an interview with The Verge , adding that an alleged spy would potentially be interested in “better understanding what the US government is thinking on export controls,” as well as gathering information on Huang’s conversations with the Trump administration, attempting to influence policy, and gathering information on trade secrets like “who’s buying Nvidia’s chips, who’s getting them first, what’s coming next in terms of AI chips.” Megaspeed’s sister company, headquartered in Malaysia, spent $4.8 billion or more on Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and February 2026, the Times reported, citing trade records from trade platform ImportGenius. The transaction sizes were outside the norm for a small company, particularly when Nvidia chips are so difficult to get. ”Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job” Nvidia spokespeople had said Huang’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was strictly business. Their interactions were described as “not unusual or unexpected” in statements to the press. Nvidia’s line was, “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.” But at some point, their relationship became personal. In June 2024, just before Megaspeed became an Nvidia customer, photos show the two with other AI executives at a bar in Taipei after a local trade show; the following year, they reportedly had a business dinner in Taipei with others as well. But in private, according to US officials cited by the Times , the two’s relationship raised alarm bells for the US government — they had reportedly been surveilling the Megaspeed executive for months, if not longer, and that’s how it came out that she was in close contact with Huang. The revelation is particularly concerning because of Huang’s lobbying role. He’d been trying to convince the Trump administration and Congress to loosen export controls for sending advanced semiconductors to China, ostensibly so that Nvidia could sell more chips. We now know this was happening around the same time that Huang was spotted at the Taiwan dinner with Alice Huang in May 2025, according to Culper Research , which shorted Nvidia’s stock earlier this year. That dinner occurred shortly after Nvidia had shared the Trump administration’s new restrictions on its China-specific H20 chips in April. Just a couple months after the Taiwan dinner, Huang reportedly met with Trump in the Oval Office in July 2025 to plead his case for loosening export restrictions on Nvidia’s advanced semiconductors. Days later, the company announced that the administration had blessed sales of its H20 chips to China. Huang had argued that spreading American chips to China would help establish US technology as the standard, rather than allowing for Chinese chips to grow, according to The New York Times . After setbacks earlier in the second Trump term in export policy to China, Huang began speaking with then-White House AI czar David Sacks in 2025, who became the key advocate for Nvidia’s view that selling American chips to China would be beneficial, the Times reported. By October 2025, Huang was lobbying Trump to allow Nvidia to sell more advanced chips to China, ahead of Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, per the Times ; but after Trump considered the proposal , he ultimately decided not to move forward. (That same month, Huang hired an external PR firm known for handling sex scandals, Wired reported.) Months later, in December 2025, Trump changed course slightly, allowing Nvidia to sell H20 chips to a greenlit list of “approved customers” in China, with the US government taking a 25 percent cut of those sales. The same rules would apply to other US chipmakers, he wrote on Truth Social at the time. “It is in Nvidia’s interest and in Jensen Huang’s interest to lobby for looser export control restrictions” CSET’s Dohmen said that during the past two years, the US has seen a light loosening of AI export control regulations under the Trump administration, driven partly by Huang’s own lobbying. But it’s important to note, she said, that “even without any kind of intelligence operations from the Chinese side, it is in Nvidia’s interest and in Jensen Huang’s interest to lobby for looser export control restrictions.” Any restrictions by definition stifle Nvidia’s business expansion and cut off potential sales to help it grow its already stunning market cap — which is currently about $4.25 trillion, second only to Apple. Huang’s relationship with Trump is also particularly relevant here. The president lavished praise on Huang during a speech last year, saying that until recently, he hadn’t even heard of Nvidia, and then he wanted to break it up. But after meeting Huang, he said, he understood why it would be difficult to re-create the company he’d built. More recently, Huang put Trump on speakerphone when the president called him during an appearance onstage at the All-In Summit, publicly displaying his close access to the Oval Office. This past spring, a classified memo — the writing of which was overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, per the Times — circulated among Trump administration officials ahead of the president’s trip to China in May, warning of the Megaspeed executive’s alleged involvement in surveillance on behalf of China’s Ministry of State Security. Her reported goal was to learn about advanced AI chips in the US and try to influence them being made available to China on a large scale. Asked if he had known about the memo reviewed by Rubio at a press briefing on Monday, Trump said, “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” Earlier in the briefing, he said he was unaware of the alleged spy connection ahead of his trip to China. Huang was initially left off the list of executives joining Trump on the trip, but the president later asked him to join . Trump had been briefed about a year ago that US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive to be a China intelligence operative, according to the Times , and that she had a close relationship with a US citizen who turned out to be Nvidia’s CEO. At the time, he reportedly chose not to take action. So far, the allegations haven’t affected Huang’s future at Nvidia. He’ll continue to lead the company during the investigation. Trump has also stood by him since news broke of the affair, telling reporters this past weekend, “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.” Nvidia said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised” On Sunday, Huang wrote an internal memo to Nvidia employees — some of which are his own family members — writing, “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He then addressed Nvidia’s board, partners, and shareholders, adding that he is “fully committed” to leading the company and “will work to earn back your confidence.” This weekend, Nvidia’s board of directors launched an independent investigation into the national security allegations. Huang will not have control over the participants in the investigation, and Nvidia said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello wrote in a note on Monday that Morningstar “can’t rule out the investigation fading away and Nvidia returning to business as usual,” particularly since Huang is the “only CEO the company has ever known.” There’s also the fact that Huang’s Nvidia struck deals in August with six large financial institutions to provide more than $500 billion in financing for the buildout of AI data centers and other infrastructure, and as the US-China AI race intensifies, those are high-stakes agreements. “It’s unclear to us what these partnerships and financing deals would look like with a different Nvidia CEO,” Colello wrote. “Costs of capital may rise for future investments if perhaps the most prominent CEO in the AI landscape is no longer orchestrating such deals.” Morningstar still maintained a very high uncertainty rating for the company, with Colello writing that it’s possible US approval of Nvidia to sell H20 chips to China will be revoked and that the company could ostensibly be sanctioned as well. Trump told reporters on Sunday that Huang should remain CEO of Nvidia and that he would “certainly take him” on his next trip to China. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump told reporters. “He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.
