to Pave the Way for AI in Finance In the financial sector, the utilization of real-world data faces significant constraints due to strict privacy regulations, compliance requirements, and the need for advanced domain expertise. In this context, the development of agentic AI in the financial domain requires synthetic data capable of avoiding the risks of using real data while reflecting demographics, household structures, and asset statuses to reproduce diverse, realistic financial scenarios. To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan , a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset " Nemotron-Personas-Japan ." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs , a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer , an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA). This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development . The Nemotron-Personas collection , including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework NeMo User Sim , enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world. What’s in the Dataset? 9M personas total (1M records x 9 personas each), written in natural Japanese 50 fields per record : 9 persona fields, 11 persona attributes, and 30 contextual fields based on official demographic and labor statistics ~1.5B tokens total , including ~750M persona tokens ~950k unique names 1600+ occupation categories reflecting Japan's workforce Comprehensive coverage across demographic, regional, asset distribution, and personality trait axes Diverse persona types : Occupations, sports, arts, travel, cooking, finance, financial behavior, and financial concerns Natural language persona attributes : Cultural background, skills and expertise, career goals and aspirations, hobbies and interests, household/parental/financial background, attitudes toward money, and financial planning Available for both commercial and non-commercial use under the CC BY 4.0 license How We Built It Data Generation Pipeline It was built using NVIDIA’s framework for synthetic data generation, NeMo Data Designer . This compound AI system enables complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and support for multiple generation backends. This is the essential toolset required for generating such large-scale synthetic datasets. In addition, the following models were utilized: NeMo SDG-PGMs (Apache-2.0) : A probabilistic graphical model framework for statistically grounded data generation gemma-4-31B-it (Apache-2.0) : For Japanese text generation Enhanced Cultural Context Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan was designed to align with Japan's official demographic and labor statistics while taking into account key considerations essential for AI training: Education : Where national statistics broadly aggregate degree levels, we introduced finer granularity to enable the model to reflect diverse educational pathways. Occupation : We incorporated additional categories (such as business owners and specialized professions) to broaden the spectrum of occupations used for training. Life Stages : We modeled scenarios that rarely surface prominently in statistics, such as students, retirees, and periods of unemployment, to represent more realistic personas. Household Finances : In addition to individual income and spending propensity, we incorporated household-level financial and real assets to replicate diverse economic backgrounds. Digital & Financial Literacy : By including internet and smartphone usage along with financial literacy, we enabled the model to precisely capture consumer profiles in financial use cases. Private By Design Every persona is fully synthetic. No real individuals are represented, and the dataset is designed to reduce privacy risk. Demographics and household finances follow official statistics and public survey data, and names follow real Japanese naming patterns. Personas are built from these distributions, not from records about real people. Who This Data Is For Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan is built first for teams creating financial AI in Japan, at banks and insurers and at the startups and integrators that serve them. Each persona carries household finances and financial literacy alongside demographics. Teams can use them to build customer-service agents, evaluate sales conversations/marketing initiatives, run user simulations in NeMo User Sim, and red-team customer-facing AI. The release also serves anyone building for Japanese users. It holds 9M personas, 50% more than Nemotron-Personas-Japan, across 50 fields instead of 22. That gives any Japanese-language project finer slices of the population to train and test on. Practical AI Applications The synthetic personas in this dataset can be leveraged for: Multi-turn conversation : Using personas as "seeds" to generate human-like dialogue datasets. Domain-specific AI development : Generating datasets to build AI assistants tailored to realistic scenarios in financial use cases. Bias testing and fairness : Evaluating how models and AI agent systems perform across rural and urban divides, various age groups, educational backgrounds, and economic circumstances to check whether AI performs consistently across Japanese society. Why It Matters Access to diverse, high-quality training data that reflects real-world populations has long been a challenge in AI development. Enterprise AI development has predominantly relied on private data, creating barriers for researchers, startups, and particularly AI developers in regions with limited available data. Data Diversity : Reflects the full spectrum of Japan's population, which helps reduce biased training and the risk of model collapse . Cultural Authenticity : Reduces reliance on Western-centric datasets and supports the development of Sovereign AI systems . Privacy and Governance : Aligned with Japan’s innovation-first approach to AI governance. Every persona is synthetic, so no customer data is needed to build or test with it. By releasing Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan under CC BY 4.0, we provide access to enterprise-grade, high-quality synthetic data, empowering anyone to build culturally grounded AI systems with lower cost and less privacy risk. Pairs with Nemotron-PII-Japan Nemotron-PII-Japan launches the same day. It holds 100,000 synthetic Japanese business documents with labeled personal information, for training and testing detection and redaction models. Its documents are built on Nemotron-Personas-Japan. Use Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan to simulate customers, and Nemotron-PII-Japan to test how your pipeline protects their data. Start Building with Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan You can download this dataset using the command below to help develop AI that genuinely understands Japanese culture and language. from datasets import load_dataset ds = load_dataset( "nvidia/Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan" ) Use cases for building production-ready applications: Using personas as seeds for dialogue generation Fine-tuning models with culturally grounded data Building personalized engines that reflect Japan's overall demographic makeup Developing domain-specific AI agents equipped with Japanese context From teams building AI in Japan to global developers aiming for broader regional deployment, Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan dataset provides the authentic, privacy-conscious foundation required for your applications. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together Enterprise Article Published November 9, 2026 Upvote 6 Alex M Tseng alexmtseng Follow amazon Luca Zancato zancato Follow amazon :last-child]:mb-0"> Higher-Order Pruning of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models Introduction Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used. Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization . Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove. Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance . Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates. Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method. In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers . Experts don't work alone In a standard MoE, each layer has E E E experts, and each input token x x x is routed independently to K K K such experts ( K = 8 K = 8 K = 8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights g k ( x ) g_{k}(x) g k ​ ( x ) for each expert k k k , wherein the K K K experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T ( x ) ⊂ { 1 , . . , E } T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\} T ( x ) ⊂ { 1 , .. , E } . The output of the layer is then ∑ k ∈ T ( x ) g k ( x ) f k ( x ) \sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x) k ∈ T ( x ) ∑ ​ g k ​ ( x ) f k ​ ( x ) , where f k ( x ) f_{k}(x) f k ​ ( x ) is the output of expert k k k for token x x x . Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts. Importantly, experts in the selected set T ( x ) T(x) T ( x ) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature , as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout. This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately. This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous. How HOPE identifies a prune-set (See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective) When we delete a set of P P P experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T ( x ) T(x) T ( x ) (for any token x x x ) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error . Our goal is to find the prune-set P P P (of some predefined pruning budget ∣ P ∣ \vert P\vert ∣ P ∣ ) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens x x x from our calibration set). Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over P P P directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set P P P itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate Z Z Z , which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error: Z = [ ∑ j ∈ P ∩ T ( x ) g j ( x ) ∥ f j ( x ) ∥ 2 ] 2 ≥ true error Z = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error} Z = [ j ∈ P ∩ T ( x ) ∑ ​ g j ​ ( x ) ∥ f j ​ ( x ) ∥ 2 ​ ] 2 ≥ true error Because Z Z Z is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms g i ( x ) g j ( x ) ∥ f i ( x ) ∥ 2 ∥ f j ( x ) ∥ 2 g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2} g i ​ ( x ) g j ​ ( x ) ∥ f i ​ ( x ) ∥ 2 ​ ∥ f j ​ ( x ) ∥ 2 ​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard. Each entry F i , j F_{i,j} F i , j ​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts i i i and j j j , across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal F k , k F_{k,k} F k , k ​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( F i , j F_{i,j} F i , j ​ for i ≠ j i\neq j i  = j ) measure pairwise cooperative contribution. What does F F F look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer: Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores. In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates. Connection to REAP Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP) , a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of F F F recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ = 0.988 \rho = 0.988 ρ = 0.988 ). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the F F F -matrix. Results We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines ( REAP , MAN , EAN , and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%. HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B. Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank ( 2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes ( 39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes ( 67% ). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions. As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of F F F become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls. HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro , an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2 , a 13% regression). Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods . Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set. HOPE retains more cooperating experts Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree. HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix F F F . To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous. How to run HOPE We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5. Step 1: Calibrate hope calibrate \ --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B \ --prompts calibration_prompts.txt \ --out-path observations.h5 The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file. Step 2: Solve QP hope solve \ --obs-path observations.h5 \ --prune-frac 0.50 \ --out-path pruneset.json This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm. Step 3: Prune hope prune \ --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B \ --pruneset-path pruneset.json \ --out-path ./Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-pruned-50 To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed). We also released a more compact Python API: from hope.calibrate import calibrate from hope.solve import solve from hope.prune import prune_model calibrate( "Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B" , calibration_prompts, "observations.h5" ) solve( "observations.h5" , prune_frac= 0.50 , out_path= "pruneset.json" ) prune_model( "Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B" , "pruneset.json" , "./Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-pruned-50" ) Limitations of HOPE HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate. title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
description: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation. Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth. “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator. He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says. And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.” He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk. “Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.” Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI. But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation. Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth. “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator. He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what's going on,” he says. And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.” He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk. “Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.” Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI. But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.” Deep Dive Artificial intelligence Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. content: AI Policy Tech The future of AI hinges on… Jensen Huang’s sex life? NVIDIOT. NVIDIOT. by Elizabeth Lopatto Nov 9, 2026, 5:36 PM UTC Step 1. Cut a hole in the box. Image: The Verge Part Of Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang see all updates Elizabeth Lopatto is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg. I would prefer that these people’s sex lives were none of my business but I guess we have to talk about Jensen Huang and the National Security Incident. Who could have guessed that the guy who was out here signing titties might not have great judgment about how to behave around women ? Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — is a former TV reporter. That was before she became “an executive” at Megaspeed, which bought $4.8 billion of hard-to-get Nvidia chips, starting around the time she was being photographed with Jensen in a Taipei bar in 2024. “To many in the industry, the well-funded push by Megaspeed into A.I. appeared to come out of nowhere,” The New York Times wrote, tactfully . Our girl Alice is also an alleged honeypot who was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security. ( China is denying all this, btw.) You know shit is going good when your corporate spokesperson has to tell the Times that of course your company does not disclose classified information to your customers What is Megaspeed? Well. The company has ties to the Chinese military and builds data centers in “Southeast Asia” (it has offices in Singapore and Indonesia) to sell compute to Alibaba. The chips it is using to do that are banned from being imported to China. Incidentally, Nvidia has been lobbying very intensely to get rid of import controls on its chips so it can sell them in China. This is all public knowledge in part because Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly “oversaw” a memo detailing Alice’s recruitment and relationship with Jensen, and then someone leaked it. (Powerful memo game, Marco, getting credit for one you didn’t even write!) Rubio passed his little note around in May, ahead of a trip to China taken by President Donald Trump. Jensen initially didn’t make the list of invitees on the trip — at least, not until Trump saw media coverage of the perceived snub. Trump and Jensen? They’re close. Which makes it even more interesting that Trump was personally briefed on the findings and did nothing, according to the Times . You know shit is going good when your corporate spokesperson has to tell the Times that of course your company does not disclose classified information to your customers. John Rizzo, the spokesman, also told the Times that Nvidia’s customers don’t ask Nvidia to lobby for changes to the chip restriction. Bit of a hat on a hat, John. First of all, they don’t have to — Nvidia’s financial incentives do it for them. Second, imagine this is a regular company. The business model of Megaspeed is that the chips are restricted, and that Megaspeed gets ahold of them. Megaspeed has no incentive to upend this situation! Unless, you know, it’s acting against its financial interest because it’s a front for Chinese spies… in which case, that statement is going to be embarrassing. Speaking of embarrassing, Rizzo told the Times “that Mr. Huang’s interactions with Ms. Huang were ‘not unusual’ and consistent with the kinds of meetings he has with any of Nvidia’s many customers.” Oh, okay. Who else was Jensen fucking? Nvidia has an extraordinary structure Because two days after that statement, Jensen sent the most incredible email addressed “To my colleagues at Nvidia” in which he admitted he had been “unfaithful.” Then, he wrote, “To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.” Are… your wife and family on the Nvidia employee email list? Well, yes! His son is a director of product management; his daughter is a senior marketing director. He even gave a job to his son-in-law! Also, Nvidia has an extraordinary structure. Jensen has 60 direct reports. Leave aside that there is no possible way to manage that many people well. I would like to direct your attention to something else entirely: If he is in trouble, there is no part of the company that is untouched. The usual problems attain, of course — he was in a position to have gotten any information she might have requested! He could have left company laptops available for infiltration! But because of the structure, he also could have issued commands to his many direct reports that benefited the CCP. Neat! I sure hope someone who knows a lot about cybersecurity is going through Nvidia with a fine-toothed comb. Is he in trouble? Well, Nvidia is opening an investigation into Jensen, who is also its largest individual shareholder . (At least there’s no dual-class stock !) Nvidia shares are, as of this writing, down almost five percent, which seems like an underreaction. I don’t know where Jensen’s actual wife, Lori, is in all this Perhaps more consequentially, the Democratic Party just swept back into power and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) seems mad . Also, the voters hate the data centers that house Nvidia chips , and I notice a lot of ambitious politicians thinking about the next presidential elections. For instance, there’s Rubio’s name attached to the memo . I also notice Trump’s popularity is at an all-time nadir. Besides any Democrats positioning themselves for a run, a Republican looking to create some daylight between himself and Trump could easily do so by going to town on Jensen, who is Trump’s buddy. I do not think Rubio is the only ambition monster to worry about. I don’t know where Jensen’s actual wife, Lori, is in all this. They got married in 1985. She gave up her job as a microchip designer to raise their kids. I would be very surprised if there is a prenup. I would be somewhat surprised if there was a postnup. Jensen doesn’t own as much of Nvidia as Jeff Bezos did of Amazon when he cheated on and divorced his wife, but it’s something to keep an eye on, if Lori decides she’s out. We’ve talked once or twice about Nvidia’s central role in the AI ecosystem — and specifically, that it is heavily involved in financing AI neoclouds. It has investments in SpaceX, CoreWeave (where it was, as of the time of the IPO, the company’s second-biggest customer) , and OpenAI, among others. Jensen has been promoting “compute as an asset class.” Nvidia is, effectively, the central bank of AI One of the reasons I have been uncertain about when and how the AI bubble will pop is that it seems to me that Nvidia can bail out any or all of these companies anytime it needs to, just like it did for CoreWeave when its IPO was threatened. Neoclouds exist because Nvidia wanted to create competition for its chips, so its biggest customers — Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Oracle — couldn’t exert too much pricing pressure. Certainly I am not the only person who has noticed that Nvidia is, effectively, the central bank of AI . If Nvidia is in a particularly bad way, it kind of seems like, at minimum, the neoclouds get fucked too. Oddly, CoreWeave is up about 6 percent as of this writing; the stock market moves in mysterious ways. Maybe that is why our nation’s foremost thought leaders on X are posting things like “Whomst among us hasn’t accidentally fucked a Chinese spy? That’s how it is on this bitch of an earth.” I’m kidding, here’s investor/loudmouth Bill Ackman : “ We should all support him and his family. Onward .” Shaun Maguire, partner at VC firm Sequoia : “I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” (Elon Musk took a quick break from complaining about Dave Chappelle’s comedy to type “ I agree ” to Maguire’s note.) So Jensen can’t go down, as there’s no one who can replace him, and Nvidia can’t go down, as nothing can replace it. The AI industry better hope there isn’t some further revelation coming that would make one of these things unavoidable, such as the investigation finding proof that Alice directly accessed Nvidia’s systems while Jensen was showering or something. Might also be bad if, say, a US Commerce Department inquiry into Megaspeed was halted after Nvidia intervened . Didn’t we just hear somewhere that Jensen had been influencing the Trump administration’s policy on export controls ? Anyway, as of this note, Jensen isn’t planning to step down as CEO . Might as well settle in for the most fun we’ll have until we find out that Musk did IVF with a family member of Chinese President Xi Jinping. The Walt Disney Company has teamed up with Adobe to develop proprietary “artist-led” generative AI models to support Disney’s production pipeline. The multiyear partnership was announced today at Adobe’s MAX conference, and it will see Adobe providing Disney with early access to its latest technologies for everything from Disney’s theme parks and cruise line to ESPN content. Adobe will contribute to “expand internal creative workflows” at Walt Disney Studios and identify how AI can be used to shape ESPN content and “enhance the engagement with sports fans.” This is the latest example of Disney embracing generative AI tools, following a previous deal with OpenAI and involvement with Character.AI’s bankruptcy . title: Medium’s new TK app brings AI assistance directly into the writing process
description: Medium's new writing app embraces AI-assisted writing, despite growing controversy over the technology's role in publishing.
content: Online publishing platform Medium on Monday launched a new app, called TK, which aims to bring AI technology deeper into the writing process. The idea behind TK is to make it easier to turn ideas into written words by incorporating an AI assistant into the editor itself, allowing users to ask for help by typing “@TK” followed by their request or prompt. In publishing and journalism, the term “TK” serves as a placeholder used to mark where missing information can be added later. The “TK” stands for “to come,” but uses a “K” instead of “C” as there are few English words where the “tk” letter combination exists, making it stand out more easily in written text where it could be caught by proofreaders. In Medium’s app , TK takes on a new role as it tries to help users fill in the blanks. The company suggests the AI assistant could help answer questions that you might normally have to switch to another tab to quickly look up, like how many days are in a particular month. The app could also pull in bits of writing you had previously saved to the app when you were still fleshing out your ideas. In addition, Medium says TK will ship with particular skills for editorial feedback, headline feedback, and others that could match your draft to the style guide for Medium publications. Medium’s move to embrace AI in the early stages of writing could prove controversial at a time when the publishing and literary worlds have been reckoning with the role that artificial intelligence has played in the creation of new long-form prose. Multiple authors have lost book deals over suspicions that they used AI technology to help them write, while other literary awards have come under scrutiny after winners were suspected of writing with AI assistance . While writers have long used automated tools for proofreading and light grammatical edits, there is growing concern across the publishing industry that an AI assistant’s editorial “suggestions” can become the writing itself, instead of being reflective of the thoughts in the writer’s own mind. But because AI models were trained on human writing, there are also questions around the reliability of AI detection tools in terms of their ability to properly determine when something was written with AI, rather than with its assistance, versus not at all. TK leans into this debate, taking the side that these nuances will ultimately no longer matter in the end. Instead, the company celebrates what AI can bring to the world of writing, saying that “artificial intelligence makes writing more important, not less,” and proclaiming that “AI is a technology that has the power to amplify human intelligence and it uses the written word as a foundation.” Image Credits: Medium (TK app) Still, Medium concedes that AI does raise the possibility of low-quality content and blurring the line between what’s human-written versus AI-written. To address these concerns, TK allows authors to publish notes that transparently explain how AI was used in their writing. “This is a start of what we believe is required to publish in the AI era, which is to make the provenance of writing clear, transparent, and inspectable, right down to the prompting and source material,” Medium explained in a blog post about the launch. In addition to writing assistance, TK will help users remember and organize what they had previously written and suggest writing prompts. The app can also optionally connect to your own AI agent through TK’s MCP server or Claude skill, so the app can better understand your projects, your positions, and other ideas that could be stored in your agent’s memory. Meanwhile, the new app incorporates human feedback in a social layer, the company says, allowing writers to share their early drafts with others and get feedback. At launch, TK is available on the web, but a desktop app is on the roadmap, Medium says. The app can import and export Markdown, but it’s not a Markdown app itself. The writing in TK is also not encrypted, as the app is designed for collaboration, but users will be able to set access control permissions on their work. Medium, which is profitable, says TK will be a free tool for those with a Medium account. title: Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50”
description: Nvidia’s board is investigating Jensen Huang over his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, and Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld thinks it’s roughly a coin flip whether Huang stays on as CEO.
content: Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. But this isn’t a case of just another CEO having an extramarital affair. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry ,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down. A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “ groundless smears and slanders ,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and it isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised. The question is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought. First, the damage. Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted. But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.” Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits , if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that people earn latitude in a group by showing competence and following its rules. Huang has been earning latitude since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. But all that goodwill can run out when a screw-up looks self-serving or touches the group’s core norms. Here that group includes Nvidia’s board, its roughly 42,000 employees who are bound by security rules, and, in a looser sense, the U.S. government, given it restricts its exports. We also talked about precedents, except, as it turns out, there really are none for what’s unfolding right now. Executives who survive personal scandals sometimes pick up where they left off at another company, Sonnenfeld observed. Former HP CEO Mark Hurd is one example. Between 2005 and 2010, he drove HP to the top of the tech industry by revenue, then was pressured to resign after he filed inaccurate expense reports that hid a personal relationship with a contractor. Oracle hired him about a month later. Huang has no equivalent because Nvidia is his company As for the bench at Nvidia, that doesn’t really exist either. While there is typically a hierarchy inside companies of Nvidia’s scale and importance, Huang has kept things as flat as possible, with about 60 direct reports by his own account. That structure makes it hard to figure out who would succeed him (though his children, both of whom work at Nvidia, are sometimes the subject of succession speculation ). That won’t stop the worldwide guessing game that’s sure to follow. And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea. Nvidia’s role at the center of a massive and complex circular financing web is what makes this particular predicament so tricky and, undoubtedly, terrifying for a wide number of constituents. Nvidia isn’t just the biggest provider of chips driving the AI boom but also largely the bank behind the buildout. In addition to stakes in hundreds of smaller startups, Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave and Nebius. In August, it also signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion over time, and Huang has said Nvidia could backstop up to a quarter of it. The move was widely interpreted as a way to spread risk. Still, a leadership crisis at the center is how a stumble becomes a collapse. So what’s Nvidia’s board likely doing right now? Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s constant, public advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, whose company Nvidia has backed, had a lot to say about selling chips to China at Davos back in January, likening it to “ selling nuclear weapons to North Korea .” Now the board’s independent members — meaning everyone but Huang — will have to establish what technology reached China if any, and by what routes, including by better understanding Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed. The Singapore cloud company, which grew out of a Chinese gaming business and became Nvidia’s largest buyer in Southeast Asia, bought roughly $2 billion of its chips , the New York Times reported in October 2025, raising broader questions about whether it was helping China circumvent U.S. export restrictions by re-exporting the chips to China or renting them to Chinese customers remotely. (An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill after the Times report that the allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year .”) In the meantime, Huang will keep running the company, Nvidia said Sunday. That’ll be a tall order, even for a CEO who already spends much of his time traveling the world to promote Nvidia. For starters, three House chairmen want a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18. Nvidia is also reporting its newest earnings on November 17. Sonnenfeld expects that even if Huang keeps the title, he’ll have to hand off some of the day-to-day decision-making. Only one thing is certain right now. Huang doesn’t own the kind of super-voting stock that would cement his power at Nvidia. Sonnenfeld often argues for dual-class structures that empower founders, and he says Huang’s success without one has been the best counterargument to that case. But if Huang had one, Sonnenfeld continued, removing him would be harder. This episode may be remembered as a pivotal moment for how the tech industry guards its secrets. Sonnenfeld argues tech has been “way too lax” compared with defense contractors that face clearance regimes. The arrest last month of an OpenAI engineer points to the same problem. He was accused of hiding a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room, and while OpenAI has said it has no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were accessed, the case highlights how exposed tech companies are to people who get close. Huang may well survive the investigation (Sonnenfeld hopes the board clears him of knowingly aiding anyone). The bigger test comes when Nvidia’s employees, customers and partners, and, indirectly, the millions of Americans with Nvidia in their 401(k) plans, have to decide whether an AI economy built largely on the judgment of Huang still makes sense. The Effect Builder bot is available on the web to build whatever new Instagram filters you can think of. by Stevie Bonifield Nov 9, 2026, 6:07 PM UTC Image: Instagram / Meta Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI. After expanding its Edits app to macOS last week, Instagram’s next move is launching this Effect Builder that generates custom filters for your Stories posts with AI. Available now for US residents who are over 18, it has a prompt box for describing your filter idea to the chatbot, with an option to attach style reference images. Then you can upload your own photos to preview the AI-generating effects, and ask for changes in follow-up prompts. There’s also an option to allow Instagram’s AI to rewrite your prompt, which turned my one-line test prompt “Make a filter that turns photos into comic book pages” into several AI-generated paragraphs of detailed style requests on everything from color palette to lighting. The filter Effect Builder generated as a result still looked nearly identical to its output for my original one-liner. 1/2 Instagram’s AI rewrote my prompt into lengthy, detailed instructions. Screenshot: The Verge / Instagram You can submit your filters to Instagram directly from Effect Builder, but effects have to pass a safety review before they’ll be available to other users. Instagram says after an effect is approved, it “shows up in Instagram Stories for anyone to use, and whenever someone uses your effect we’ll link back to your profile so that it’s easy for others to find your work.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
description: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance. Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. “Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers. These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands. Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.” This webcast is produced in partnership with Infosys.
